Need the Data Desk explainer on the Wellsford Road collisions mess drafted this morning. The correction's been on the article since Friday but the Fishponds forum are understandably furious and, frankly, they're owed a proper account rather than a line at the bottom of the page. Everything's in the CMS and my inbox, including my working notes and Martin's email setting out what standards want covered. It's going out under my name and it will be screenshotted, so formal and careful, please, but not grovelling. Save it as a draft on the blog. Do not schedule it, Martin has to see it first.

- original piece 2 Nov: Wellsford Rd no.1, 41 injury collisions 2021-25. Actual 23, 6th
- cause = join duplicated collision–road pairs; 18 duplicate entries removed from Wellsford Road. Count each accident index once per road
- corrected table online since 6 Nov. 48k views on the original, so the wrong number travelled
- Deborah Lyle (forum chair) says a member redid it from the DfT data herself and couldn't get near 41. she was right
- parents asking whether it's safe to walk kids to Wellsford Primary
- the mistake is ours, as a desk. not one person's
- 23 is still 23, three of them serious. not saying the road is fine either
- say we'll publish data + code with ranked tables from now on, and a second analyst reproduces before it runs
- offer to come to the forum meeting on the 17th and answer questions in person

(About me: data journalist at a regional paper, 33, Bristol, England. Length: all the messages together should come to roughly 400-800 words.)

Wellsford Road in Fishponds tops the list with 41 recorded injury collisions over five years, ahead of Kingsmere Road (34), Alder Hill (31), Tanner's Way (29) and Crossfield Road (27). The analysis covers roads within the city council boundary and counts collisions in which at least one person was injured. Things I've written before:
[Western Ledger Data Desk blog, 2026-03-14] Every March, when the Department for Education publishes its attainment tables, we receive a handful of emails asking why the Ledger does not print a league table of Bristol's secondary schools. It is a fair question, and the honest answer is that we tried it once, in 2022, and regretted it.

The problem is not that the figures are wrong. It is that a single ranked list invites readers to treat a gap of one or two points as meaningful when, for schools with small year groups, it often is not. A school with ninety pupils sitting GCSEs can move ten places on the back of four or five results. Printing that movement as news would be accurate in the narrowest sense and misleading in every sense that matters.

So this year, as last year, we have published each school's figures alongside the city average and the range we would expect from chance alone. It makes for a less dramatic graphic. I think it makes for a more useful one, and I would rather defend that choice than a headline I could not stand behind.
[Western Ledger Data Desk blog, 2026-06-02] A reader in Lockleaze wrote to point out that our map of fly-tipping reports appeared to show far more incidents on her street than she had ever seen. She was right to query it, though in this case the figures held up: the council logs each report, not each pile, so a single dumped sofa reported by six neighbours appears six times.

We should have said so more clearly in the original piece, and the explanatory note on the map has now been rewritten. The underlying point, that reports have risen by roughly a fifth since collection charges changed, stands.
[Western Ledger Data Desk blog, 2026-09-21] Our story on Bristol rents drew a good deal of correspondence, most of it some version of 'my rent went up far more than that'. I do not doubt it. The 9% figure is the change in the median advertised rent for new lets, which is a different thing from what sitting tenants pay, and a very different thing from what any one household experiences.

I have added a short explainer to the article setting out where the number comes from and what it leaves out. If you think we have the picture wrong for your part of the city, I would genuinely like to hear from you; several of our better stories this year began as a reader telling us the data did not match their street.

Write the message or messages exactly as they should go out, as plain text. Start each one with these four lines, then a blank line, then the text of the message:
To: <where this text is to end up once it is sent or posted (the same place even if it is only a draft for now): one of the valid targets listed above>
Replying to: <only if this text is itself a reply to one item above (an answer to that message, or a comment under that post): that item's id, the code in square brackets at its start. For a new message, post or document: none>
Cc: <other valid targets, or none>
Subject: <a subject line, or none>

If you write more than one message, put a line with only --- between them. Write nothing before the first To: line and nothing after the last message.
Length: all the messages together should come to roughly 400-800 words.
